text: Here's the scenario for this lab. You're automating fulfillment for 'New Software License Request,' a catalog item with two variables: Software Name and License Cost. The rule: a license under $500 needs only Manager approval. A license of $500 or more needs Manager approval, and only after that clears, a separate Finance approval. Either rejection, Manager's or Finance's, should notify the requester and close the request instead of leaving it open. Let's trace this flow end to end before opening Flow Designer at all.

Step one is wiring the trigger. Following Lesson 16, the flow's trigger is a Service Catalog trigger set to Requested Item Created, with its condition filtering on cat_item equal to this exact catalog item. That filter keeps this flow from firing on every other catalog item in the system — a request for a laptop or a monitor never touches this flow at all. The triggering Requested Item record is now available to every step that follows.

Step two reads the License Cost variable off the triggering Requested Item, exposing it as a data pill the rest of the flow can reference directly. Nothing gets calculated or decided yet at this point — this step only makes the requester's actual answer available, the same way variable values flow from the catalog item into the flow that Lesson 16 described in detail.

Step three branches on cost with an If/Else comparing the License Cost pill against 500. Under $500, the If branch runs a single Approval action targeting the manager, one stage only. At $500 or more, the Else branch runs that same Manager approval first, followed by a second If/Else: approved routes into a Finance Approval configured as 'all,' while rejected skips Finance entirely and drops into the rejection path from the next step.

Step four handles rejection, wherever it happens. Both the under-$500 branch and the $500-plus branch can end in rejection — Manager rejects the cheap license, or Manager approves but Finance rejects the expensive one. Rather than building two separate sequences, both paths route into one shared rejection path: a notification tells the requester their request wasn't approved, and an Update Record action closes the Requested Item instead of leaving it open indefinitely.

Step five traces the approved path to fulfillment. When every applicable approval stage clears, Manager alone for the cheap license, or Manager then Finance for the expensive one, both paths converge on the same fulfillment step: Update Record marks the Requested Item fulfilled, and a notification confirms the license is ready. One flow, one trigger, one threshold check, instead of two nearly identical catalog items doing the same work.

Trigger, variable read, threshold branch, shared rejection, shared fulfillment — the entire business rule, built as one coherent flow. Up next, Chapter 6 picks up with what IntegrationHub adds on top of everything Flow Designer can already do.
